text: From 1952 to 1969 the US Air Force officially investigated more than 12,000 UFO sightings under Project Blue Book.
explain: True. Most were explained; a few hundred were never identified.

text: The Pentagon ran a secret programme to study UFOs, revealed in 2017.
explain: True. It was called AATIP, the Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program.

text: In 2020 the Pentagon officially released three Navy videos of "unidentified aerial phenomena".
explain: True. They're often called the "Tic Tac", "Gimbal" and "GoFast" videos.

text: The US government didn't officially admit Area 51 existed until 2013.
explain: True. It was acknowledged in declassified CIA documents.

text: In 1977 a radio telescope in Ohio picked up a strong 72-second signal from space that has never been conclusively explained.
explain: True. It's the "Wow! signal", named after what the astronomer scribbled next to it.

text: In 1997 thousands of people in Arizona saw huge formations of lights in the sky.
explain: True. It's known as the Phoenix Lights. The military later said at least some of them were flares.

text: In 1561 a printed news sheet in Nuremberg reported crowds watching orbs, crosses and cylinders "battling" in the sky.
explain: True. It's one of the most famous early "UFO" reports.

text: The US government funded "psychic spies" to do remote viewing from the 1970s until 1995.
explain: True. It was known as Project Stargate.

text: In the 1960s the CIA tried to implant a microphone in a cat to eavesdrop.
explain: True. It was called Operation Acoustic Kitty and it didn't work.

text: In the late 1950s the US Air Force studied detonating a nuclear bomb on the Moon.
explain: True. It was Project A119, intended as a show of strength during the space race.

text: During WWII, the psychologist B.F. Skinner trained pigeons to guide missiles by pecking at a target on a screen.
explain: True. It was Project Pigeon. The pigeons were good at it, but it was never used.

text: In WWII, Britain spread the story that carrots gave its pilots night vision.
explain: True. It was a cover story to hide the fact that they were using radar.

text: In WWII, a US Army unit used inflatable tanks and fake radio chatter to fool the enemy.
explain: True. It was known as the Ghost Army.

text: During the Cold War, the CIA secretly helped promote American abstract art.
explain: True. It worked through front organisations, to show off "American freedom".

text: In 1924 the major light bulb makers agreed to limit bulbs to about 1,000 hours of life so people would buy more.
explain: True. It was the Phoebus cartel.

text: In the 1960s the sugar industry paid Harvard scientists to play down sugar's role in heart disease.
explain: True. The scientists blamed fat instead, and the documents came to light in 2016.

text: In 2017 Apple admitted it had been slowing down older iPhones.
explain: True. It became known as "Batterygate" and Apple later settled lawsuits over it.

text: Volkswagen used secret software to cheat on emissions tests.
explain: True. The "Dieselgate" scandal broke in 2015.

text: Two young cousins faked photos of fairies that fooled the Sherlock Holmes author Arthur Conan Doyle.
explain: True. These are the Cottingley Fairies. The cousins admitted the hoax in 1983.

text: In 1932 the Australian army was sent with machine guns to deal with emus, and the emus essentially won.
explain: True. It's known as the Great Emu War.

text: In 1978 22 French air traffic controllers watched a radar blip fly over Paris at 6,000 mph before vanishing.
explain: True. The incident was officially investigated by GEIPAN, France's government UFO agency.

text: Between 1989 and 1990 thousands of people in Belgium reported seeing silent, low-flying black triangles, prompting the Air Force to scramble fighter jets.
explain: True. Known as the Belgian UFO wave, it remains officially unexplained.

text: In 1977 the Brazilian Air Force launched a secret mission called Operation Saucer to investigate glowing lights allegedly attacking locals in the Amazon.
explain: True. Hundreds of pages of photographs and sketches were declassified decades later.

text: In 1986 the crew of a Japan Air Lines cargo flight reported being followed over Alaska by three giant glowing objects.
explain: True. Radar data backed up parts of the crew's account.

text: In 1945 Soviet schoolchildren gifted the US Ambassador a wooden carving of the US Seal that secretly hid a battery-free listening device.
explain: True. Known as "The Thing", it hung in the ambassador's Moscow residence for seven years before being discovered.

text: During the Cold War, the Soviet Union mapped the entire world in extreme detail, including secret military bases and bridge weight limits in Western cities.
explain: True. Soviet military maps were often more accurate than local street maps.

text: In the 1960s the Soviet Union trained bottlenose dolphins to detect underwater mines and enemy divers.
explain: True. Both the USSR and the US ran military marine mammal programmes.

text: In 1962 a laughter epidemic broke out in Tanzania, affecting around 1,000 people and forcing 14 schools to temporarily close.
explain: True. The Tanganyika laughter epidemic lasted for several months.

text: In 1518 hundreds of people in Strasbourg, France, danced uncontrollably in the streets for weeks, with some collapsing from exhaustion.
explain: True. It's known as the Dancing Plague of 1518.

text: In 1958 China launched a nationwide campaign to wipe out sparrows because they ate grain, which accidentally triggered a locust plague and famine.
explain: True. It was part of the Four Pests campaign.

text: In 1964 a Swedish journalist exhibited paintings created by a chimpanzee under a fake French artist's name, and a critic praised the "delicate" brushwork.
explain: True. The artist "Pierre Brassau" was actually Peter, a four-year-old chimp from Borås Zoo.

text: In the late 1970s the South African military ran a secret programme attempting to turn gay soldiers straight using aversion therapy.
explain: True. Known as the Aversion Project, it was exposed after the end of apartheid.

text: In 1988 Italian scientists published a paper claiming water could "remember" substances dissolved in it even after being diluted to nothing.
explain: True. Jacques Benveniste's "water memory" study caused a massive scientific scandal.

text: In 1995 a Tokyo doomsday cult secretly manufactured sarin nerve gas and released it on the city's subway system.
explain: True. Aum Shinrikyo carried out the attack, shocking Japan and the world.

text: During WWII, Polish soldiers adopted a Syrian brown bear named Wojtek, officially enlisting him as a private so he could travel with them and carry artillery shells.
explain: True. Wojtek was eventually promoted to corporal and retired to Edinburgh Zoo.

text: In 1978 Argentina sent a pregnant woman to Antarctica so her baby would be the first human born on the continent, strengthening their territorial claim.
explain: True. Emilio Marcos Palma was born at Esperanza Base in January 1978.

text: During the Vietnam War, the US military secretly seeded clouds over the Ho Chi Minh Trail to extend the monsoon season and wash out supply routes.
explain: True. It was called Operation Popeye, and led to an international treaty banning weather warfare.

text: In 1989 Pepsi briefly became the sixth-largest military power in the world after the Soviet Union traded 17 submarines and three warships for Pepsi syrup.
explain: True. Pepsi promptly sold the fleet to a Swedish company for scrap metal.

text: In 2007 the Swiss Army accidentally marched 170 armed soldiers across the border into Liechtenstein during a storm before realising they were in the wrong country.
explain: True. Switzerland apologised, and Liechtenstein took it in good humour.

text: In the 1960s the Canadian government funded a device nicknamed the "Fruit Machine" to try to identify gay civil servants by measuring their pupil dilation.
explain: True. It didn't work, though thousands of people still lost their jobs during the "Lavender Scare".

text: In 1966 a group of Tongan schoolboys stole a boat, got shipwrecked on a deserted island, and survived together peacefully for 15 months until rescued.
explain: True. Unlike "Lord of the Flies", they set up a commune, tended a garden, and cared for a boy who broke his leg.

text: In 1919 a massive storage tank burst in Boston, sending a 25-foot wave of molasses rushing through the streets at 35 mph.
explain: True. Known as the Great Molasses Flood, it killed 21 people and flattened buildings.

text: During the Cold War, the CIA smuggled banned copies of the novel "Doctor Zhivago" into the Soviet Union to spark anti-communist sentiment.
explain: True. They even printed miniature editions designed to fit inside coat pockets.

text: In 1974 archaeologists in China uncovered an army of over 8,000 life-sized terracotta soldiers buried to protect the tomb of the first Emperor.
explain: True. Local farmers stumbled upon the Terracotta Army while digging a well.

text: In 1999 NASA lost a $125 million Mars orbiter because one engineering team used metric units while another used imperial inches and feet.
explain: True. The Mars Climate Orbiter burned up in the Martian atmosphere.

text: In 1923 a jockey named Frank Hayes won a horse race in New York despite having suffered a fatal heart attack mid-race.
explain: True. He stayed in the saddle until his horse crossed the finish line.

text: In 1954 a Japanese fishing boat was showered with radioactive ash from a secret US hydrogen bomb test at Bikini Atoll, inspiring the creation of Godzilla.
explain: True. The crew of the "Lucky Dragon No. 5" fell severely ill, sparking massive anti-nuclear protests in Japan.

text: In 2011 a woman in Sweden accidentally found her lost wedding ring 16 years later growing around a carrot in her garden.
explain: True. She had lost it while baking in 1995 and dropped it into vegetable peelings used for compost.

text: In 1986 Lake Nyos in Cameroon suddenly released a massive cloud of deadly carbon dioxide gas, suffocating over 1,700 people in nearby villages overnight.
explain: True. It was a rare natural disaster known as a limnic eruption.

text: In 1904 the Olympic marathon in St. Louis nearly killed the winner after officials gave him rat poison and brandy as performance enhancers.
explain: True. Thomas Hicks was carried across the finish line by his trainers and survived.

text: In 1974 NASA quietly added a "greeting chamber" to the Skylab space station in case astronauts met aliens.
explain: Made up. No such room existed on Skylab.

text: A 1952 US Air Force study found most UFO sightings happened on Tuesdays and recommended grounding pilots that day.
explain: Made up. Project Blue Book was real, but this finding wasn't.

text: After a Scottish fishing town all reported the same glowing triangle in 1983, the Ministry of Defence paid each resident £50 to stay quiet.
explain: Made up. No town was ever paid to keep quiet.

text: The Voyager Golden Record sent into space originally included a recipe for apple pie, which was removed at the last minute.
explain: Made up. The Golden Record is real, but it had no recipes.

text: In 1979 a Canadian university offered a degree in "Extraterrestrial Diplomacy", and three students graduated.
explain: Made up. Nobody has graduated in alien diplomacy, yet.

text: During the Cold War, MI5 trained hedgehogs to carry listening devices under the hedges of embassy gardens.
explain: Made up. The CIA's cat was real; MI5's hedgehogs were not.

text: In WWII, Britain trained parrots to memorise and repeat German radio codes.
explain: Made up. Pigeons were used in WWII; parrots weren't.

text: The KGB ran a fake ballet school in Paris to recruit dancers as spies.
explain: Made up.

text: In the 1970s the Pentagon funded research into whether soldiers could be kept awake for a week by playing recordings of laughter.
explain: Made up. The psychic spies were real; this wasn't.

text: In 1962 the Soviet Union trained seagulls to spot American submarines.
explain: Made up.

text: In the 1950s chewing gum makers secretly agreed to make gum lose its flavour faster so people would buy more.
explain: Made up. The light bulb cartel was real, though.

text: In 1931 pencil manufacturers agreed to make erasers wear out before the pencil did.
explain: Made up.

text: In 1971 a British tea company secretly switched to smaller leaves so its bags brewed weaker and people would use two.
explain: Made up. If it were real, there'd have been a revolution.

text: In 1965 umbrella makers agreed to weaken the spokes so umbrellas would break in strong wind.
explain: Made up. Umbrellas just break on their own.

text: In 1890 a Belgian town was gripped by uncontrollable hiccups that lasted six months.
explain: Made up. A laughter epidemic happened in Tanzania in 1962, though.

text: In 1932 the British Army was sent to a Scottish island to wipe out rabbits, and the rabbits won.
explain: Made up. The Emu War was real; the Rabbit War wasn't.

text: In 1956 a Dutch village set all its clocks to run backwards for a year as a protest.
explain: Made up.

text: In 1964 a Harvard psychologist taught a whole term without ever appearing in person. Students only heard his voice, and their exam scores went up.
explain: Made up. It's a nice idea, though.

text: In 1974 Swedish researchers paid volunteers to watch the same film every night for a month to see whether they'd fall asleep sooner each time.
explain: Made up. The only thing it would have proved is that the film was boring.

text: In the 1960s a Swiss linguist claimed bilingual people dream in a third, invented language, and the government funded a five-year study into it.
explain: Made up. Bilingual brains do mix languages, though. It's called "code-switching".

text: In 1981 the French space agency accidentally broadcast a live cheese-making tutorial into deep space instead of a peace message.
explain: Made up. If aliens ever reply, it'll probably be "wrong number".

text: In 1992 the Japanese government secretly funded a robot designed solely to bow slightly lower than foreign diplomats.
explain: Made up. Polite, though.

text: In 1973 Italian pasta makers held a secret summit in Naples to shorten spaghetti by two centimetres so people would eat bigger portions.
explain: Made up. A secret Italian summit would have leaked within minutes.

text: During the 1980s East German border guards used trained badgers to detect people digging tunnels under the Berlin Wall.
explain: Made up. Guard dogs were used, not badgers.

text: In 1968 an Australian weather station accidentally mistook a massive flock of migrating pelicans for a classified Soviet weather balloon.
explain: Made up.

text: In 1954 the Brazilian Navy spent three months firing warning shots at a floating iceberg that turned out to be a giant rogue foam mattress.
explain: Made up.

text: In 1976 Swiss watchmakers secretly agreed to make all quartz watches run three seconds fast per month so people would buy newer models.
explain: Made up. Quartz watches are famously accurate.

text: In 1985 a town in rural Spain banned whistling after residents became convinced it attracted stray weather balloons.
explain: Made up.

text: In 1969 Indian railway officials tested whether playing classical sitar music at stations would make commuters walk faster onto trains.
explain: Made up. Though classical music is used to deter loitering in some stations today.

text: In 1977 Denmark's meteorological institute quietly deleted February 30th from an old archive to cover up a forecasting mistake.
explain: Made up. Sweden actually did have a February 30th in 1712, though!

text: In 1988 a South Korean electronics firm built a prototype TV that turned itself off if it detected the viewer had fallen asleep.
explain: Made up. Sleep timers exist, but not mind-reading TVs.

text: In 1961 a Norwegian fishing village convinced tourists that a local fjord contained a rare "square-shaped" herring.
explain: Made up.

text: In 1972 Mexican archaeologists briefly classified a buried 1950s hubcap as an ancient Aztec sun disc before realising their mistake.
explain: Made up.

text: In 1984 New Zealand's postal service trained border collies to sort parcels by sniffing out different types of glue.
explain: Made up. Clever dogs, but not that clever.

text: In 1967 a Viennese coffee house ran a secret experiment replacing decaf with regular espresso for a month to see if philosophers wrote faster.
explain: Made up. The philosophers would have just argued about whether the experiment was real.

text: During WWII, the Swiss Army trained St. Bernard dogs to carry tiny barrels of fondue to stranded mountain patrols.
explain: Made up. Brandy barrels were a myth too—St. Bernards never carried barrels at all.

text: In 1982 Argentina secretly built a giant papier-mâché aircraft carrier in the South Atlantic to fool British satellite surveillance.
explain: Made up. Inflatable tanks were used in WWII, not fake carriers in the 80s.

text: In 1971 the Soviet Union briefly traded 500 snowploughs to Cuba in exchange for three million crates of mangoes.
explain: Made up. Though Pepsi really did get Soviet warships.

text: In 1994 Iceland's government passed a law requiring all new roads to curve around large boulders in case they housed hidden elves.
explain: Made up. Road projects have occasionally been altered due to local folklore, but there's no actual law.

text: In 1963 a Canadian research team built a machine designed to detect lies by measuring changes in a person's ear temperature.
explain: Made up.

text: In 1928 a molasses factory in Antwerp exploded, coating the city's tram tracks and halting public transport for three weeks.
explain: Made up. The Great Molasses Flood happened in Boston in 1919, not Belgium.

text: During the Cold War, East Germany smuggled secret anti-Western messages inside sheet music exported to Viennese orchestras.
explain: Made up.

text: In 1987 a Mongolian postal service experiment tested using trained golden eagles to deliver urgent telegrams between remote yurts.
explain: Made up. Eagles are used for hunting there, not post.

text: In 2003 the European Space Agency lost a probe because one team programmed coordinates in degrees while another used percentage gradients.
explain: Made up. NASA did lose a Mars orbiter over metric vs. imperial units, though.

text: In 1951 an Egyptian museum curator accidentally locked himself inside a sarcophagus overnight and was rescued after tapping Morse code on the lid.
explain: Made up.

text: In 1979 Peru's tourism board briefly hired lookalikes to pose as ancient Incan guards at Machu Picchu to boost visitor numbers.
explain: Made up.

text: In 1965 a French cheese company secretly funded a study claiming Camembert improved short-term memory before exams.
explain: Made up. If it worked, every student in France would have found out by now.

text: In 1983 a Finnish sauna manufacturer recalled 4,000 units after discovering the thermostats were calibrated in Kelvin instead of Celsius.
explain: Made up. 350 Kelvin is about 77°C, which would actually still work!

text: In 1959 a Portuguese fishing village held a three-day trial for a seagull accused of stealing the mayor's pocket watch.
explain: Made up.

text: In 1991 a South African diamond mine briefly shut down after workers refused to enter a tunnel they believed was haunted by a Victorian opera singer.
explain: Made up.
